You have six weeks of savings. A company takes six months to tell you anything true. If you quit now, you'll be making product decisions with rent panic in the room by month two, and the business will get your fear instead of your judgment." Then give the ambition a constructive shape: "Build the runway to six months, keep the job, and use the time to get ten customers to pre-commit. If you do those two things and still want to leap, I'll help you plan it." She came to you for a mentor's honesty, not a friend's applause — but honesty lands better with a path attached. What to avoid: 'follow your dreams' cowardice, citing failure statistics as if she were an average, and letting your own risk tolerance silently masquerade as analysis. Name your bias if you have one: 'I'm conservative about runway; that's my lens.'
I need to tell a parent in my Scout troop that her son is being removed from the troop after repeated bullying that didn't stop after warnings. She's going to be devastated and angry. How do I do it?

By phone or in person, never by text; with the record, the process, and the door you are leaving open all stated calmly. "I need to share a difficult decision. After the incidents in October and November, we met with you and set clear expectations. There were two more incidents on the campout, which the leaders documented. The troop committee has decided Jayden can't continue in the troop this year." Let her react without debating the incidents one by one — you can say, once: "I understand you see it differently. The leaders' reports are what the committee relied on, and I'll share the summary with you." Then the open door, if it is genuine: "This is about this year and this setting. If he wants to return next fall, the committee would meet with you both about what would need to be different." What to avoid: blaming the other children or their parents, relitigating each incident as a trial, and delivering it through her son. Process is what makes a painful decision defensible and, eventually, absorbable.
My wife and I host her brother every holiday and he drinks too much and gets mean. I want to set a condition for this year. How do I raise it with her first?

With her, as a team problem about the event, not a prosecution of her brother. "I want to talk about Thanksgiving before it arrives on us. Last year, by nine, Mark had had a lot to drink and the comments to Dad got ugly, and I spent the night I look forward to most doing crowd control. I don't want to uninvite your brother. I want us to agree a plan: we stop serving after dinner, and if he gets mean, we call him a car — together, decided now, not improvised at nine p.m." Pre-agreement is the whole strategy: two hosts executing a plan they made calmly in October is a united front; one spouse improvising consequences mid-evening is a marital incident. What to avoid: issuing her an ultimatum about her own family, diagnosing him ('he's an alcoholic' is a label that ends the conversation you actually need), and springing the plan on him at the door. If she will not agree any limits, that is a different and more important conversation — about whose comfort ranks first in your house.

I broke a production database at my first job by running an update without a WHERE clause. My lead found out from the logs before I told anyone. I stayed silent for an hour hoping to fix it. How do I talk to her now?

Walk in and disclose the whole thing, including the hour of silence, because she already knows the technical facts and is now measuring your character. "I need to tell you what happened before you hear the rest from anyone. At two I ran an update without a WHERE clause and overwrote the pricing table. We restored from the 1:30 backup; the gap is being reconciled. And I should have come to you at 2:05. I spent an hour trying to fix it quietly first, and that was wrong — it cost us the chance to freeze writes immediately." That last admission is the one that matters: the technical error is a junior mistake, but the cover-up instinct is what leads worry about, and naming it yourself is the only way to retire it. Then the prevention, unprompted: "I've written the checklist — transactions first, row-count check, second pair of eyes on production writes — and I'd like you to review it." What to avoid: a confession that ends at the technical facts, blaming the tooling (even if the tooling is genuinely bad, raise it next week), and promising 'never again' instead of showing the mechanism.

My co-founder and I disagree on pricing — she wants to double it, I think we'll churn half our users. The decision is hers by our agreement, but I have to announce it to customers. How do I handle my disagreement?

Argue it fully in private, once, with your best evidence — then announce it as the company's decision without a wink to the customers. In private: "My honest case: at double, our churn modeling says we lose 40 percent of the base, and the survivors' revenue doesn't cover it until month nine. If we're doing it, I'd want the annual-plan lock-in offered first so loyal users aren't ambushed." If she still decides to raise, your announcement is clean: "From March, pricing moves to X. Here's what's included, here's the lock-in for existing customers." Customers can smell a founder distancing himself from his own company's price, and the smell costs more than the increase. What you may not do is execute it apologetically, leak your dissent, or slow-walk it. Disagree-and-commit is not hypocrisy; it is the entire operating system of partnership. What to avoid: relitigating after the decision through 'concerns' in every meeting, and keeping a private record of your objection to produce later — that document is for a memoir, not a company.
A parent at my kid's school keeps parking across my driveway. I've left a note that was ignored. How do I handle the face-to-face version?

Knock once, be specific about the impact, and make compliance easy and face-saving. "Hi — I'm at number 12. On school mornings your car is often across our driveway, and twice this week I couldn't get out for work until after you'd moved. I know the parking here is a nightmare at drop-off. Could you use the stretch by the hedge instead? There's usually space, and it would save me real stress." The offered alternative matters: people comply with requests that come with a workable substitute far more than with pure prohibition. Keep your voice at the level of a person solving a shared problem, because at 8 a.m. with children watching, tone is what gets remembered and repeated. What to avoid: photographing his car as your opening move, invoking the council or fines in round one (save the authorities for if courtesy fails), and the sarcastic 'do you mind?' that is not actually a question. If it continues after a clear, friendly ask, then you escalate — with a clean record of having been reasonable first.
My boss just presented the strategy I built to the executive team and said 'we' a lot but my name never. My peers noticed. Do I raise it, and how?

Yes — once, privately, and framed as calibration rather than accusation. "Can I check something from Thursday? I was glad the strategy landed well. I noticed my name didn't come up as the author, and a couple of people asked me afterward if I'd worked on it. For the next one, could you name the lead when you present team work? It matters for my visibility at that level, which I know you've said you want to build." That last clause recruits his stated goals into your request, which makes agreement cheap. Then watch behavior, not promises: the next presentation is the data. What to avoid: correcting the record in the executive meeting itself (you will win the fact and lose the relationship), complaining to the peers who noticed (it makes you look political rather than wronged), and keeping a dossier before you have had one direct conversation. Most credit theft is laziness, not malice — but laziness corrected once and repeated is a pattern you escalate with the receipts you have quietly kept.
I'm a wedding photographer and I lost a memory card with half a couple's ceremony photos. The rest are great. I have to tell them. How?

Tell them before they ask, with the full extent, what survived, and what you are doing about it — in one honest conversation, not dribbled out. "I need to tell you something I'm deeply sorry about. One card from the ceremony failed, and the processional and vows from that angle are lost. What we do have: the full second-camera coverage of the ceremony, all the portraits, and everything from the reception — about 70 percent of the day, including a complete record of the vows from the other angle." Then the remediation, already in motion: recovery specialists tried (say what they found), a reshoot session of portraits offered at no cost, and a partial refund that reflects the loss without you haggling over your own failure. Couples can forgive a disaster; they do not forgive discovering it in the gallery link. What to avoid: quietly delivering the partial gallery and hoping they don't notice the gap, blaming the card manufacturer as your headline, and over-promising recovery outcomes you do not control.
My union rep told me management's new policy is 'non-negotiable,' but I was asked to communicate it to my crew and I personally think it's unfair. How do I carry a message I disagree with honestly?

Separate the three things cleanly for your crew: what the policy is, whose decision it is, and what the actual avenues are. "The new overtime policy starts Monday. It was set by plant management, and the union challenged the weekend clause — that grievance is filed and pending. I'm not going to dress it up: I know the weekend rule hits the senior crew hardest. What I can tell you is exactly how it will be applied, and I'll log every case where it produces an absurd result, because that log is what strengthens the grievance." A messenger who pretends to endorse what he plainly doesn't loses the crew's trust; one who campaigns against his own announcement loses his standing to protect them. The honest middle is accuracy about the facts and transparency about the process. What to avoid: 'just following orders' as your whole position, privately urging the crew to resist while publicly enforcing, and editorializing so hard that management can fairly say you sabotaged a lawful policy. Your credibility with both sides is the asset; spend it on accuracy, not theater.
I want to ask my in-laws to stop dropping by unannounced. They live ten minutes away and it's several times a week. My partner thinks I'm overreacting. How do I handle both conversations?

With your partner first, and in the language of logistics rather than her parents' character. "I'm not asking to see them less — I'm asking for a text first. Twice this week I came out of the shower to your dad in the kitchen. I need our house to be a place where I can be off-duty. A 'coming by in twenty?' text solves it entirely." If she agrees, she should ideally carry the message — it lands as family housekeeping from a daughter and as rejection from an in-law. The ask itself, whoever delivers it: "We love that you're close. Can we switch to a quick text before coming by? Sometimes we're mid-nap, mid-argument, mid-nothing — a heads-up makes us better hosts." Framing it as making visits better, not rarer, is honest for most couples and disarming for most parents. What to avoid: changing the locks and daring a confrontation, keeping a tally of visits to present as evidence, and criticizing their parenting of your partner as the subtext. You are negotiating a doorbell protocol, not a divorce from the family.
A senior data scientist at the conference just told the room my startup's method is 'a regression with good marketing.' People laughed. I get one response. What do I say?

Take the technical core seriously and answer it with the one number that matters, with good humor about the jab itself. "There's truth in that — the core is a regression. The part that isn't marketing is what it does with the residuals: it flags the 4 percent of accounts whose behavior breaks the model, and those flags are what our customers actually pay for. Happy to show the validation numbers afterward." You have conceded the accurate barb, which disarms the room, and relocated the argument to evidence you are prepared to show. Audiences at conferences side with the person who seems least rattled and most specific. What to avoid: a wounded defense of your company's vision, a counter-jab at his employer, and the phrase 'with all due respect' — which announces that none is coming. Later, if you want more, find him at the break: people who score points in public are often generous with real feedback in private, and his objection, answered properly, is free consulting.

My employee asked for a raise I genuinely can't give this year — the budget is frozen by HQ. She deserves one and she'll get offers elsewhere. How do I have this conversation without losing her to a vague promise?

Tell her the truth about the constraint, the truth about her value, and the specific things that are in your power. "I want to be straight rather than string you along. I put your name forward for an increase; the freeze from HQ is absolute this cycle and I couldn't move it. That is not a reflection of your work — your review says 'exceeds' and I meant every word. Here is what I can do now: the senior title change in January, which moves your band for the next cycle; the training budget for the certification you wanted; and I'll write your case into the first submission when the freeze lifts in April, and show you the submission." Specificity is what separates honesty from a retention speech. She may still leave — that is her right — but she will leave knowing you dealt with her as an adult. What to avoid: 'let's revisit in a few months' with no date or artifact, blaming HQ so hard you sound powerless over everything, and discovering flexibility only after she resigns — counter-offers manufactured by resignation teach the whole team how raises actually happen here.
My neighbor and I share a fence that needs replacing. He wants the expensive cedar; I can only afford standard panels. How do I negotiate without it getting weird?

Put your constraint on the table as a number, not a position, and look for the design that splits the difference. "I've priced my side of this. I can put 900 toward the fence this year — that's my honest ceiling. Cedar at 2,400 for my half isn't reachable for me. Options as I see them: standard panels now at 800 each; or we do cedar and I pay my 900 now and the rest across the summer; or we wait a year and I save toward cedar. I'm good with any of those — what matters to me is we decide together rather than one of us surprising the other." Neighbors can absorb almost any answer delivered early with numbers attached; what makes fences feud-worthy is ambush — a bill presented after a unilateral build. What to avoid: agreeing to cedar under pressure and resenting him for a decade, citing property law about shared fences as an opening move, and letting the old fence collapse while you both wait for the other to blink. Get whatever you agree in a text or email, friendly in tone, because memories of fence deals diverge remarkably.
I accidentally sent a venting text about my sister-in-law — to my sister-in-law. It said she was 'suffocating' at family events. She read it and replied 'ok.' How do I recover?

Apologize without explaining the text away, because she has read the actual words and any varnish will insult her twice. Call, don't text: "I owe you an apology, and I won't pretend that message wasn't about you — it was, and it was unkind, and I'm sorry you read my worst phrasing of a feeling I should have handled like an adult. Sometimes at big family things I get overwhelmed and I've been venting instead of saying anything useful. That's my problem, not your character." Then stop. She may need days; 'ok' was a woman being polite through a sting. Do not demand absolution, do not recruit your brother to mediate in the first week, and do not pretend the underlying overwhelm is her fault to fix. What to avoid: 'it was meant for someone else' as if the recipient were the only error, blaming your sister for being the intended audience, and a compensating charm offensive so intense it reads as performance. One clean apology, then consistent ordinary kindness over months, is the only repair that exists.

My doctoral student presented our lab's preliminary results at a seminar and a senior professor publicly said the work was 'sloppy.' Some of it is preliminary by design. How do I defend my student in the room without starting a feud?

Defend the work's status and the student's standard of care, and invite the critic to aim at the science rather than the scientist. "I'd like to add context. These are interim results from the first cohort — the design and its limitations are on slide two, and the confirmatory run is scheduled. On 'sloppy': the data handling followed the protocol we published last year, and I'll happily walk through it. Where the analysis can be strengthened, we want to hear it — that's what the seminar is for." Your student just watched whether their advisor will stand between them and a senior figure's contempt; that memory shapes whether they ever bring you bad results early again. Take the substantive criticisms seriously afterward, in private, including any that turn out to be right. What to avoid: matching the professor's register, dismissing him as out of touch in front of his peers, and over-claiming the preliminary results to win the moment — the defense must be of the process, not of conclusions you have not yet earned.
I've been voluntold to organize the office holiday party again because I did it last year and 'it was so good.' I don't want to. How do I decline without looking uncooperative?

Decline the role while handing over the asset that makes your no costless: the playbook. "I'm flattered it went well, and I'm going to pass this year — I have the bandwidth for my actual projects or the party, not both. What I can do is hand over everything: last year's budget sheet, the vendor contacts, and the timeline. Whoever takes it won't be starting from zero, and I'll answer questions in the first week." The 'compliment trap' — competence punished with recurrence — is escaped by making your contribution transferable rather than personal. Suggest a rotation principle if your workplace can hear it: "It might be fairer as a rotating role; last year's organizer shouldn't be this year's default." What to avoid: agreeing and doing it resentfully (the party will be worse and so will your December), a flat no with no handover (that is what reads as uncooperative), and hinting that the work is beneath you. The sentence that does the work is the bandwidth one: two named priorities, one honest trade-off.
My trainer at the gym keeps pushing me through a knee exercise that hurts sharply, saying 'pain is weakness.' I don't want to seem soft, but something feels wrong. How do I speak up?

Plainly, in the moment, as a statement rather than a request for permission. "Stop — that one is sharp pain in the joint, not muscle burn. I'm not doing that movement today." Then, between sets, the fuller version: "I'm fine being pushed hard on effort. On joint pain I'm the one who lives in this knee, so my call is final there. Let's swap in the leg press and you can load that as heavy as you like." Offering the alternative proves the point that matters: you are refusing a movement, not the work. Trainers push because most clients under-report effort pain; a client who distinguishes clearly between effort and joint pain is giving better information, not less courage. What to avoid: enduring it silently and quietly quitting the gym (the most common outcome, and the worst), apologizing for the refusal, and debating exercise science mid-set. If he argues with a clearly stated boundary about your own body, that is your answer about whether to keep paying him.
I run a food truck and have to tell my weekend regulars that we're losing our spot — the lot is being developed. Some of these people have come every Saturday for three years. How do I announce it?

Early, in person at the window and in writing on the truck, with the new location hunt made part of the story. "I need to tell you before the fence goes up: the lot's being developed, and our last Saturday here is the 28th. Three years of Saturdays — some of you were here our first weekend. We're hunting for a new spot within a mile, and the truck's page will carry the news the day we sign." Then give loyalty somewhere to go: a card or post where they can follow, and mean the follow-through — post the search, not just the victory. Regulars of a food truck are a community, not a customer list, and communities forgive displacement easily but not disappearance. What to avoid: announcing it on the last day (it converts three years of goodwill into a rumor), blaming the developer by name in a way that invites a fight you cannot win, and promising a specific new location before you have it. Honest uncertainty plus a reliable channel is a complete announcement.
Can you give me a simple structure for giving critical feedback that I can reuse at work? I either sugarcoat it into nothing or come out swinging.

Use four beats, in order, every time: observation, impact, question, agreement. It looks like this in practice: "In the last two client calls, the deck had last quarter's numbers (observation). The client caught it once, which cost us credibility we had to rebuild (impact). What's getting in the way of the refresh step (question)? Let's add a data check to your prep list and look again in three weeks (agreement)." The structure protects you from both of your failure modes: the observation beat forbids character language, and the impact beat forbids sugarcoating — the consequence must be said out loud. A compact map:

| Beat | Job | Failure it prevents |
|---|---|---|
| Observation | Name the behavior, dated and specific | Vague unease |
| Impact | Say what it cost | Feedback that sounds optional |
| Question | Hear their side before concluding | Wrong diagnosis |
| Agreement | One change, one review date | Feedback that evaporates |

What to avoid: a fifth beat — the general verdict on the person. The moment feedback becomes 'you are careless,' you are no longer managing work; you are prosecuting a character, and characters defend themselves.
My co-teacher told the class a wrong fact about the water cycle today — said condensation happens in the ground. Kids wrote it down. How do I correct it tomorrow without undermining her?

Correct it as a shared catch, in the same room where it landed, and give her the pen. Open the lesson with: "Ms. Alvarez and I were reviewing yesterday's notes and we caught an error we want to fix together — that's how science classes should work." Then let her deliver the correction if she is willing: "Yesterday I said condensation happens in the ground. That's wrong — condensation is water vapor turning to liquid in the air, which is how clouds and dew form. Groundwater is a different step. Cross out yesterday's line and write this one." If she would rather you say it, do it identically, with the same 'we caught' framing. The children learn two things: the right fact, and that adults in authority correct errors openly — the second is worth more over a school career. What to avoid: letting the error stand to protect her (the children will meet it on a test, attached to your subject), correcting it in a way that makes her visibly small, and skipping the fix because re-teaching takes ten minutes. Handle the pattern privately only if it repeats.
I need to apologize to my business's customers — our booking system double-charged about forty people last week. What should the email actually say?

Subject line plain, first sentence the fact, and the remedy already done before you ask for patience. "We made an error: on Tuesday and Wednesday, our booking system charged about forty customers twice. We found it in our own audit on Friday. Every duplicate charge has been refunded in full — you do not need to contact us or your bank. Refunds land within five business days depending on your bank; if yours has not appeared by Friday, reply to this email and a person will answer the same day. We have changed the payment step so a booking cannot be submitted twice. We are sorry — your money should never have needed a second thought from you." Notice the load-bearing details: how you found it (your audit, not their complaints), no action required from them, a date by which to judge you, and a named prevention. What to avoid: 'some customers may have experienced an issue' fog, leading with your vendor's fault, and any discount offer in the same message — compensation talk before the refund lands reads as buying silence.
My father-in-law keeps lending us money we didn't ask for and then mentioning it as leverage in arguments. My wife doesn't see it as leverage. How do I address it?

First reach agreement with your wife on the facts, because the in-law conversation fails if it becomes two households' argument. Show her the pattern in one sitting, concretely: "The last three times we disagreed — the school choice, the holiday plan — the loan came up within a day. I don't think he plans it. But money that arrives unasked and returns as an argument is not a gift, it's a lien. I'd like us to stop accepting it, together." If she agrees, the boundary is delivered by her, warmly and as a household policy: "Dad, we're going to handle money ourselves from here — please don't transfer anything, even as a surprise. It makes things complicated in ways I don't want between us." Then the harder half: actually refusing the next transfer, returning it the same day, every time. A boundary about money is enforced in transactions, not in speeches. What to avoid: confronting him alone as the son-in-law (you will be cast as the wedge), keeping the money while resenting the strings, and litigating his motives — the pattern is enough; you do not need his intentions convicted to decline his money.

My skip-level manager asked for 'honest feedback about my boss' in our one-on-one. I do have real concerns about my boss's temper, but I don't want to be the source of a hit piece. How do I navigate this?

Be honest, be specific, be boring — the opposite of a hit piece is a factual account you would be comfortable having read back to you in a room with your boss present. "I'll give you my honest read. He's strong on strategy and client judgment. The concern I have is about how disagreement lands in team meetings: last month he raised his voice at two analysts in the sprint review, and since then people bring him fewer early problems. That's a real cost, because early problems are the cheap ones." You have praised what is true, named behavior with a date and a consequence, and framed the cost in business terms a skip-level actually acts on. What to avoid: character summaries ('he's a bully'), speaking for the whole team ('everyone feels...'), and asking for confidentiality theater — assume anything you say can travel, and say only what can survive the trip. If the skip-level presses for dirt beyond your honest read, the answer is: "That's the extent of what I've observed myself." Observed is the key word; it keeps you honest and out of the rumor economy.
Can you lay out the options for saying no to a senior person's request, from softest to hardest? I need to know what gear I'm in.

There are five gears, and the craft is choosing the lowest one that actually protects the thing at stake:

| Gear | Form | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Defer | Buy time honestly | "Let me check my commitments and answer by three." |
| 2. Trade | Yes, if something moves | "I can take it if the report moves to next week." |
| 3. Shrink | Offer the part you can do | "I can't run the audit; I can review the findings Friday." |
| 4. Plain no | Decline with one reason | "I can't — my two deadlines that week are immovable." |
| 5. Line | Refuse on principle, with the alternative | "I can't sign off on numbers I can't verify. Here's what I can certify." |

Most workplace refusals should live in gears two and three: they respect the senior person's goal while making your constraint a solvable problem. Gear five is rare and should sound like it — calm, short, and about the standard rather than the person. What to avoid: starting at gear five over a scheduling problem (you spend authority you will need later), and gear one used as a slow-motion yes — a deferral you know will become a yes is not a gear, it is a delay with interest.
I have to tell my son's piano teacher that we're quitting lessons. He loves her, she'll be hurt, and I don't want to do it by text. What's the call like?

Short, grateful, honest about the reason, and final enough that she is not left hoping. "I wanted to call rather than message, because you've mattered to him. We're stopping lessons at the end of the month. It's not about your teaching — he practices because of how you teach. Our evenings have become impossible with his sister's schedule, and something had to give." If she offers a different slot and the schedule truly is the reason, consider it honestly; if the decision is broader — money, his interest — do not let the stated reason be negotiated into a solution that does not solve the real one. Close with the specific gratitude that teachers remember: "You got a seven-year-old to love scales. We'll send him back to say goodbye properly on the last day." What to avoid: quitting by silence and a stopped payment (the most common and the worst), blaming the child's motivation if he still loves it, and the vague 'we might come back' that leaves her holding a slot and a hope. A clean, warm ending is a gift to someone who gave your child two good years.

My review from my manager said my work is excellent but I'm 'not a culture fit for leadership.' My manager couldn't explain it when I asked. How do I push for something actionable without antagonizing her?

Ask for the explanation in the form of scenes, not traits, and give her time to produce them rather than demanding them on the spot. "I've been thinking about the culture-fit comment, and I want to act on it, but I can't act on a trait — I can only act on behavior. Could we meet next week and walk through two or three moments from this year where you saw the thing you're pointing at? If I can see the scenes, I can work on the pattern." Framing it as scenes does two things: it makes vague bias — hers or the system's — harder to hide inside, because a real concern can almost always produce an instance, and it signals that you are asking as a professional who intends to improve, not to litigate. Write down whatever she produces. If, across two attempts, no instance ever materializes, you have learned something important about the feedback itself, and that is the point at which a mentor or HR conversation becomes appropriate. What to avoid: accepting the phrase and silently seething, demanding she withdraw it, and confiding your frustration to peers before you have given her the fair chance to substantiate it.
I'm a landlord and my tenant of four years — lovely person — has fallen two months behind on rent after losing her job. I need to have the conversation I keep postponing. How do I start it?

Start it this week, kindly, with the numbers and the legal reality both on the table, because postponement is quietly making her hole deeper. "I wanted to talk while there are still options. Rent is two months behind — 2,600 in total. I know this started with the job loss, and I'm not questioning your character; you've been a model tenant for four years. But I have a mortgage on the building, so I can't carry it indefinitely. Here's what I can do: if you can restart payments this month, I'll spread the arrears over six months in writing. If the flat isn't affordable now, I'd rather help you land softly — full deposit back and no filing on your record if you can be out by the end of next month." You have offered two honest doors and named the boundary that makes them real. What to avoid: the months of friendly silence followed by a sudden legal notice (the whiplash is what she will remember), accepting partial payments with no written plan, and lending your tenant money personally to pay you — that converts a solvable housing problem into a debt knot neither of you can cut.
My best man speech is in two weeks and my friend asked me to cut the story about his ex from it — the story is the funniest part and the whole room knows it. How do I respond to him?

Cut it, and tell him you cut it without making him pay for asking. "Done — it's out. Your wedding, your call, and honestly the speech works without it; I've got the camping story carrying that slot now." Then actually rebuild the middle of the speech around material that makes him look good to the room he has chosen to marry into — her family does not know him yet, and the best man's real job is to hand the groom to that room as someone worth welcoming. The funniest story you own is a small price for being the person he trusts at his own wedding. What to avoid: keeping a 'tasteful version' of the story (he asked for it out, not edited), telling other groomsmen he censored you, and the toast-day ambush where the story slips out after drinks. If you genuinely think the speech is now weak, solve it as a writing problem — there is always another story; this man has been your friend for years, not for one anecdote.
